rationale: A wins by being a little more disciplined with the facts. Its best line, "On says its subscription closes the loop on shoe waste. It hasn't said how much of the loop closes," turns the actual disclosure gap into the story without decorating it. B is sharp, but "The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" tries to manufacture a trend from one supplied product fact. That's not fatal, but it is where the draft starts doing PR jazz hands.
gaps_in_A: "get answers to the first two questions before drafting anything" over-narrows the next step around recycling proof; the ownership/category angle mainly needs price, terms, geography, and pilot learning.
"people who have already done a full cycle" assumes the pilot produced accessible full-cycle subscribers; the update only says there was a limited pilot.
"Story type: funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the public-company angle. The shape is equities/business-model materiality, not funding.
The sustainability proof list asks for "the recycling rate" but misses pilot return rate and independent verification, both central to whether the loop closes at national scale.
gaps_in_B: "The castor bean is quietly becoming a running-shoe raw material" overclaims a trend. The update supports On using castor-bean-based material, not broader adoption.
"a demand signal for an agricultural supply chain" is not earned without unit volume, sourcing, or supplier evidence.
"this model hands the retirement decision to the brand" is plausible but not grounded; the update does not say who controls replacement timing.
"The pilot has ended" is cleaner than the facts allow. The update says the subscription was previously a limited pilot, not that the pilot formally ended.
